title: Former FIFA Council member Johansen calls for Infantino to step down
dek: Isha Johansen, former Sierra Leone Football Association president and former FIFA Council member, publicly called on FIFA president Gianni Infantino to resign, citing ethical concerns over the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal and a breakdown of trust in his leadership. The statement breaks African unity behind Infantino, exposing a continental rift as UEFA and other confederations demand his departure.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Johansen, who served as FIFA Council member from March 2021 onward, told Infantino to step down for the good of football, inverting the logic Infantino used when he personally advised her to withdraw from the SLFA presidency in 2021 with the same phrase.
bottom_line: Johansen's call for Infantino's resignation marks the first major African voice to publicly break ranks with CAF's backing, though continental leadership remains officially unified behind him. Watch whether other African football officials follow her lead or whether CAF successfully isolates her as an outlier. The 2027 FIFA presidential election will test whether the financial and political pressure on African federations can overcome the ethical objections Johansen has articulated.
body: Isha Johansen, the former Sierra Leone Football Association president and former FIFA Council member, has publicly called on FIFA president Gianni Infantino to resign, citing ethical breaches in governance and a breakdown of trust. The statement breaks the unified African backing that has shielded Infantino from continental pressure and exposes a widening rift within African football leadership over his re-election bid in 2027.

Johansen's intervention carries particular symbolic weight because of her history with Infantino. She was elected to the FIFA Council in March 2021 but withdrew from the SLFA presidential election three months later, citing demands of her new international responsibilities. During that period, according to ESPN's reporting, Infantino personally visited Sierra Leone with CAF president Patrice Motsepe and advised her to step down "for the good of football." Johansen has now told Infantino to do the same, using his own language against him.

The disagreement centers on the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal, a commercial restructuring plan that Infantino advanced this year. According to ESPN, the proposal envisaged creating a commercial subsidiary valued at about $20 billion, with up to 20 percent available to outside investors, and would have consolidated FIFA's major revenue-generating operations including broadcasting, sponsorship and ticketing into the new entity. FIFA told its 211 member associations they could receive as much as $40 million each during the 2027-30 cycle if the plan succeeded, creating financial incentives for smaller federations to support it despite concerns about governance and institutional independence.

The proposal drew fierce opposition from UEFA, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation over both substance and process, per ESPN. Infantino subsequently withdrew the plan and apologized. Despite that retreat, Johansen argues the episode exposed a fundamental ethical failure. She told ESPN that Infantino should step down "for the good of football," just as she stepped down in 2021 for the same stated reason.

Johansen's position has been reinforced by Musa Bility, former Liberia Football Association president and former CAF executive committee member, who has called on CAF to reconsider its endorsement of Infantino. "Africa must not become the firewall protecting one man from accountability," Bility said, according to ESPN.

However, the official African position remains firmly behind Infantino. CAF's executive committee unanimously reaffirmed its support for his re-election in 2027, per ESPN reporting. CAF president Motsepe publicly defended him on grounds of loyalty, stating that where he comes from, people do not "stab" those who have been loyal to them "in the back." That unified stance has traditionally been Infantino's strongest shield against removal; African federations control a majority of votes at FIFA Congress.

Infantino became FIFA president in 2016 and was initially considered a lock for re-election. According to ESPN, he has now shifted from being a "shoo-in" to potentially facing pressure to resign or a challenge at the elections. UEFA is leading the push for his departure. Johansen's public break with CAF consensus signals that the African consensus may not hold as solidly as it appeared.
